title: Gastrointestinal Physiology
description: Digestion, absorption, motility, secretion, and liver–pancreas contributions to nutrient handling.

quizzes.question: A patient has reduced peristalsis after surgery but preserved segmentation. What digestive effect is most likely?
options: Forward propulsion slows while local mixing may continue.
Mixing stops entirely while propulsion accelerates.
Pancreatic enzyme synthesis ceases because peristalsis releases enzymes.
Bile is absorbed into muscle cells.
quizzes.rationale: Peristalsis propels and segmentation mixes. The two patterns support different aspects of digestion.

quizzes.question: What is segmentation’s main function?
options: Propelling contents long distances without mixing.
Mixing luminal contents and improving contact with secretions and absorptive surface.
Producing gastric acid in the colon.
Transporting portal blood to the liver.
quizzes.rationale: Peristalsis propels and segmentation mixes. The two patterns support different aspects of digestion.

quizzes.question: A patient has pancreatic exocrine insufficiency and greasy stools. Which process is impaired?
options: Bile-salt synthesis by intestinal villi.
Colonic water absorption only.
Pancreatic lipase-dependent triglyceride digestion and subsequent fat absorption.
Intrinsic-factor binding of vitamin B12.
quizzes.rationale: Pancreatic lipase contributes to triglyceride digestion. Deficiency can leave excess lipid in stool.

quizzes.question: Why can steatorrhea develop?
options: Pancreatic enzymes convert fat into hemoglobin.
Bile salts directly absorb all protein.
The stomach begins absorbing all dietary fat.
Undigested lipid remains in the lumen and is lost in stool.
quizzes.rationale: Pancreatic lipase contributes to triglyceride digestion. Deficiency can leave excess lipid in stool.

quizzes.question: A patient has reduced pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. What duodenal consequence is likely?
options: Acidic chyme is less effectively neutralized, impairing the optimal pH for enzymes and mucosal protection.
Duodenal pH rises because bicarbonate normally adds hydrogen ions.
Bile salts are no longer synthesized.
Gastric acid secretion stops immediately.
quizzes.rationale: Secretin responds to acid in the duodenum and promotes pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. This helps protect mucosa and support enzyme function.

quizzes.question: Which signal normally stimulates bicarbonate-rich secretion in response to duodenal acid?
options: Insulin released by pancreatic beta cells.
Secretin released from intestinal endocrine cells.
Renin released by the kidney.
Troponin released by cardiac muscle.
quizzes.rationale: Secretin responds to acid in the duodenum and promotes pancreatic bicarbonate secretion. This helps protect mucosa and support enzyme function.

quizzes.question: A patient has impaired bile delivery to the small intestine. Which absorption is most affected?
options: Glucose uptake stops because bile is its transporter.
Amino-acid uptake stops because bile hydrolyzes peptide bonds.
Dietary lipid absorption falls because emulsification and micelle formation are impaired.
Water cannot cross the epithelium without bile.
quizzes.rationale: Bile salts assist lipid emulsification and micelles. Pancreatic enzymes perform hydrolysis.

quizzes.question: What is the role of bile salts in normal digestion?
options: They hydrolyze triglycerides as digestive enzymes.
They directly phosphorylate glucose.
They convert protein into amino acids.
They help disperse lipid and form micelles that carry digestion products to the epithelial surface.
quizzes.rationale: Bile salts assist lipid emulsification and micelles. Pancreatic enzymes perform hydrolysis.

quizzes.question: A patient has ileal disease and loses bile salts in stool. What can occur?
options: The bile-salt pool falls, reducing micelle formation and fat absorption.
Bile production stops instantly because the ileum synthesizes all bile.
Protein digestion ceases because bile is a protease.
Gastric acid is converted into bile by colonic bacteria.
quizzes.rationale: Reabsorption conserves bile salts. Loss of recycling can lower their availability for lipid handling.

quizzes.question: Why does ileal function matter to the bile-salt pool?
options: The ileum produces all pancreatic lipase.
Bile salts are normally reabsorbed and recycled through enterohepatic circulation.
Bile salts are never recycled.
The liver receives bile salts only from the lungs.
quizzes.rationale: Reabsorption conserves bile salts. Loss of recycling can lower their availability for lipid handling.

quizzes.question: An enterocyte takes up glucose through a sodium-glucose cotransporter. What powers this uptake?
options: Direct ATP hydrolysis by the cotransporter during each transport event.
Glucose movement against its gradient by simple diffusion.
The inward sodium gradient, maintained by basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase.
Bile acids pump glucose into the cell.
quizzes.rationale: Sodium-coupled glucose uptake is secondary active transport. The basolateral pump maintains the gradient that drives it.

quizzes.question: What happens if the basolateral sodium pump is inhibited?
options: The apical cotransporter works faster without sodium.
Glucose becomes a membrane channel.
ATP concentration rises indefinitely.
The sodium gradient weakens and secondary glucose uptake declines.
quizzes.rationale: Sodium-coupled glucose uptake is secondary active transport. The basolateral pump maintains the gradient that drives it.

quizzes.question: A patient has rapid intestinal transit and watery stool. Why can water absorption decrease?
options: Reduced contact time limits absorption before contents reach the colon.
Rapid transit always increases absorption by extending residence time.
The intestine absorbs water only through muscle contraction.
Bile flow stops whenever transit accelerates.
quizzes.rationale: Water generally follows absorbed solute osmotically. Rapid transit can exceed absorptive capacity.

quizzes.question: Why does water movement follow solute transport?
options: Water is actively pumped by bile salts.
Net solute absorption creates osmotic gradients that draw water across the epithelium.
Osmosis requires an action potential.
Water cannot cross intestinal membranes.
quizzes.rationale: Water generally follows absorbed solute osmotically. Rapid transit can exceed absorptive capacity.

quizzes.question: A patient has intrinsic-factor deficiency. Which nutrient uptake is reduced?
options: Iron absorption in the colon through intrinsic factor.
Fat-soluble vitamin absorption through intrinsic-factor micelles.
Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.
Glucose uptake through pancreatic intrinsic factor.
quizzes.rationale: Intrinsic factor binds B12 and supports its uptake in the terminal ileum. Other nutrients use separate transport mechanisms.

quizzes.question: Where is the intrinsic-factor–B12 complex normally absorbed?
options: In the stomach through parietal-cell uptake.
In the colon through bile ducts.
In the pancreas through acinar cells.
In the terminal ileum through receptor-mediated uptake.
quizzes.rationale: Intrinsic factor binds B12 and supports its uptake in the terminal ileum. Other nutrients use separate transport mechanisms.

quizzes.question: A patient has low gastric acid secretion. Which digestive function may be reduced?
options: Protein denaturation and pepsin activation are impaired.
Pancreatic bicarbonate secretion becomes impossible because acid normally blocks it.
Bile synthesis stops because it requires gastric acid.
Intestinal lactase cannot be secreted.
quizzes.rationale: Acid supports protein processing but pepsin and other proteases perform enzymatic hydrolysis.

quizzes.question: Why is gastric acid not the enzyme that hydrolyzes most dietary protein?
options: It directly converts proteins into glucose without enzymes.
It helps denature proteins and activate pepsin, while proteolytic enzymes perform peptide-bond cleavage.
It emulsifies lipids by forming micelles.
It absorbs amino acids into blood.
quizzes.rationale: Acid supports protein processing but pepsin and other proteases perform enzymatic hydrolysis.

quizzes.question: A fatty meal enters the duodenum. Which hormonal response supports gallbladder emptying and pancreatic enzyme secretion?
options: Secretin is released by low blood glucose to store bile.
Gastrin inhibits pancreatic secretion after every meal.
Cholecystokinin rises in response to fat and amino acids.
Aldosterone contracts the gallbladder.
quizzes.rationale: Cholecystokinin coordinates bile delivery and enzyme secretion in response to nutrients.

quizzes.question: What does cholecystokinin coordinate?
options: Renal sodium excretion and potassium retention.
Thyroid hormone production and oxygen binding.
Colon water absorption only.
Gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion.
quizzes.rationale: Cholecystokinin coordinates bile delivery and enzyme secretion in response to nutrients.

studyNotes.title: Motility, Secretion, and Digestion
studyNotes.summary: The gut coordinates propulsion, mixing, and secretions to digest nutrients and prepare them for absorption.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Motility
Peristalsis propels contents; segmentation mixes. Enteric circuits coordinate local patterns and interact with autonomic input.

### Secretions
Gastric acid supports protein processing. Pancreatic bicarbonate neutralizes acidic chyme, while enzymes digest macronutrients. Bile salts assist lipid emulsification and micelle formation.

### Regulation
Neural and hormonal signals adjust motility and secretion according to meal composition and intestinal feedback.
keyPoints: Peristalsis propels; segmentation mixes.
Pancreatic bicarbonate buffers duodenal acid.
Bile salts support lipid micelles.
Hormones coordinate digestion and motility.
mnemonics: Propel, mix, neutralize, digest, absorb.

studyNotes.title: Absorption and Fluid Balance
studyNotes.summary: Intestinal transport moves digested nutrients, electrolytes, and water across the epithelium.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Nutrient uptake
Carbohydrates and proteins are absorbed as small molecules after digestion. Transport can use facilitated diffusion or sodium-coupled secondary active transport.

### Lipids
Bile salts support micelles; lipid products enter enterocytes and are packaged into chylomicrons for lymphatic transport.

### Water
Water follows osmotic gradients created by solute movement. The colon reclaims water and electrolytes.
keyPoints: Nutrients must be digested into absorbable forms.
Sodium gradients drive some nutrient uptake.
Chylomicrons enter lymph before blood.
Water follows absorbed solute osmotically.
mnemonics: Absorb solute; water follows.

studyNotes.title: Liver, Gallbladder, and Pancreas
studyNotes.summary: Accessory organs provide bile, digestive enzymes, and nutrient processing.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Liver and portal flow
Portal blood carries many absorbed products to the liver first. The liver processes nutrients, synthesizes plasma proteins, and produces bile.

### Gallbladder
Bile is stored and concentrated between meals, then released in response to meal-related signals.

### Pancreas
Exocrine enzymes digest macronutrients and bicarbonate neutralizes acid. Endocrine islets regulate systemic nutrient metabolism.
keyPoints: Portal flow delivers many gut products to the liver.
Bile aids lipid handling but is not an enzyme.
Pancreatic enzymes digest macronutrients.
Pancreatic bicarbonate neutralizes chyme.
mnemonics: Bile emulsifies; enzymes digest; bicarbonate buffers.

title: Endocrine and Reproductive Physiology
description: Hormone synthesis, secretion, feedback, target-organ responses, and reproductive-axis physiology.

quizzes.question: A patient has elevated cortisol followed by reduced ACTH secretion. Which feedback pattern explains this response?
options: Cortisol provides negative feedback that reduces upstream hypothalamic–pituitary drive.
Cortisol amplifies ACTH release through positive feedback.
ACTH is secreted only by the adrenal cortex after cortisol rises.
Cortisol has no effect on pituitary secretion.
quizzes.rationale: Cortisol feeds back to limit upstream secretion. Negative feedback prevents unrestrained axis activation.

quizzes.question: What is the stabilizing value of this feedback?
options: It forces cortisol to remain elevated indefinitely.
It limits excessive hormone output and helps return the axis toward a regulated range.
It eliminates hypothalamic input permanently.
It converts ACTH into cortisol directly.
quizzes.rationale: Cortisol feeds back to limit upstream secretion. Negative feedback prevents unrestrained axis activation.

quizzes.question: A water-soluble peptide hormone rapidly changes target-cell activity. Which receptor location is most likely?
options: A nuclear receptor binds the peptide after it freely crosses the membrane.
A mitochondrial receptor translates the peptide into ATP.
A cell-surface receptor relays the signal through intracellular proteins or second messengers.
A ribosomal receptor converts the hormone into DNA.
quizzes.rationale: Peptides generally use surface receptors. Intracellular signaling can rapidly alter the activity of existing proteins.

quizzes.question: Why can the response be rapid?
options: Every peptide hormone must first enter the nucleus.
The response waits for mitosis.
Receptor binding produces new hormones from ribosomes.
Second messengers can modify existing proteins without waiting for new gene expression.
quizzes.rationale: Peptides generally use surface receptors. Intracellular signaling can rapidly alter the activity of existing proteins.

quizzes.question: A steroid hormone changes gene transcription after entering a target cell. Which mechanism fits?
options: The hormone binds an intracellular receptor that regulates transcription of target genes.
It opens a voltage-gated sodium channel without any receptor.
It is translated into a membrane protein at the cell surface.
It binds hemoglobin and directly alters every organ.
quizzes.rationale: Lipid-soluble hormones can bind intracellular receptors. New gene products often take longer to affect cell function.

quizzes.question: Why may this response take longer than a second-messenger response?
options: Steroid hormones cannot cross membranes.
Transcription and translation of new proteins require time.
Intracellular receptors act only on extracellular enzymes.
Gene expression changes occur before receptor binding.
quizzes.rationale: Lipid-soluble hormones can bind intracellular receptors. New gene products often take longer to affect cell function.

quizzes.question: A fasting patient has low insulin and higher glucagon. Which liver response is favored?
options: Glycogen synthesis rises while glucose export is maximized.
Skeletal muscle exports free glucose from its glycogen stores.
Hepatic glucose output rises through glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis.
Adipose lipolysis stops to conserve fuel.
quizzes.rationale: Fasting signals favor hepatic glucose output. Muscle can use its glycogen locally but generally does not export free glucose.

quizzes.question: Why is muscle glycogen not a direct source of circulating free glucose?
options: Muscle has no glycogen.
Muscle converts all glucose into bile.
Glucagon acts only on skeletal muscle.
Skeletal muscle generally lacks glucose-6-phosphatase needed to release free glucose.
quizzes.rationale: Fasting signals favor hepatic glucose output. Muscle can use its glycogen locally but generally does not export free glucose.

quizzes.question: A meal raises insulin in a responsive tissue. Which metabolic effect is expected?
options: Glucose uptake or utilization and anabolic storage pathways are favored.
All nutrient uptake is blocked and ketogenesis rises.
Insulin converts circulating glucose directly into oxygen.
Hepatic glucose release is maximized as the dominant fed-state response.
quizzes.rationale: Insulin signals nutrient availability and supports uptake and storage. The exact response depends on tissue and receptor expression.

quizzes.question: How does insulin help lower plasma glucose?
options: It raises glucose by releasing liver glycogen.
It promotes uptake and storage in responsive tissues and suppresses hepatic output.
It prevents all glucose from entering cells.
It increases glucagon secretion from alpha cells.
quizzes.rationale: Insulin signals nutrient availability and supports uptake and storage. The exact response depends on tissue and receptor expression.

quizzes.question: A patient has low free T4 and elevated TSH with an intact pituitary. What feedback explains the TSH rise?
options: Low T4 strengthens feedback and suppresses TSH.
TSH rises only when cortisol is elevated.
Reduced thyroid hormone weakens negative feedback, allowing TSH drive to increase.
T4 directly inhibits its own synthesis without pituitary involvement.
quizzes.rationale: Low thyroid hormone weakens inhibition of the pituitary. TSH may rise as the axis attempts to stimulate the thyroid.

quizzes.question: What source normally releases TSH?
options: The adrenal cortex releases TSH.
The thyroid releases TSH into portal blood.
The kidney secretes TSH in response to sodium.
The anterior pituitary releases TSH in response to hypothalamic TRH and feedback conditions.
quizzes.rationale: Low thyroid hormone weakens inhibition of the pituitary. TSH may rise as the axis attempts to stimulate the thyroid.

quizzes.question: A patient has excess thyroid hormone and increased heat production. Which effect contributes?
options: Thyroid hormones increase metabolic activity and can enhance tissue responsiveness to catecholamines.
Thyroid hormones suppress mitochondrial metabolism in all tissues.
Thyroid hormones block every adrenergic receptor.
Thyroid hormones act only on bone and not cardiovascular tissue.
quizzes.rationale: Thyroid hormones influence metabolic rate and cardiovascular responsiveness. Clinical effects depend on level and duration.

quizzes.question: Why might heart rate also rise?
options: Thyroid hormone directly stimulates skeletal muscle troponin only.
Higher metabolic demand and enhanced adrenergic responsiveness can increase cardiovascular activity.
Heart rate is independent of endocrine state.
The thyroid converts oxygen into ATP outside cells.
quizzes.rationale: Thyroid hormones influence metabolic rate and cardiovascular responsiveness. Clinical effects depend on level and duration.

quizzes.question: A patient has high aldosterone with increased distal sodium reabsorption. Which electrolyte effect may accompany this?
options: Potassium secretion always falls as sodium is reabsorbed.
Aldosterone directly inserts aquaporins in all cell membranes.
Potassium secretion can rise in distal nephron segments.
Aldosterone blocks distal tubular transport.
quizzes.rationale: Aldosterone conserves sodium and can promote potassium secretion. Angiotensin II and potassium are important regulators.

quizzes.question: What physiologic signal can increase aldosterone secretion?
options: Low potassium and high atrial stretch only.
TSH from the pituitary is the sole stimulus.
Insulin binding to renal aquaporins.
Angiotensin II or elevated potassium can stimulate adrenal aldosterone release.
quizzes.rationale: Aldosterone conserves sodium and can promote potassium secretion. Angiotensin II and potassium are important regulators.

quizzes.question: A patient experiences a sudden stressor with an immediate heart-rate increase. Which signal contributes rapidly?
options: Sympathetic neural activity and adrenal catecholamines act quickly through adrenergic receptors.
Cortisol is the sole signal and requires new gene transcription within seconds.
Thyroid hormone is always released as the immediate response.
Aldosterone directly triggers pacemaker depolarization within milliseconds.
quizzes.rationale: Catecholamines act rapidly. Cortisol has slower genomic and metabolic effects that support sustained adaptation.

quizzes.question: What role does cortisol play relative to catecholamines?
options: Cortisol replaces all neural signaling in seconds.
Cortisol contributes to longer-term metabolic stress adaptation rather than the entire immediate response.
Catecholamines act only after days.
Cortisol is secreted by the pancreas.
quizzes.rationale: Catecholamines act rapidly. Cortisol has slower genomic and metabolic effects that support sustained adaptation.

quizzes.question: A patient’s glucose falls during fasting. Which pancreatic response supports glucose restoration?
options: Beta-cell insulin secretion rises to suppress hepatic output further.
Pancreatic amylase is converted to glucagon.
Alpha-cell glucagon secretion rises and promotes hepatic glucose production.
Somatostatin stimulates muscle glucose uptake.
quizzes.rationale: Falling glucose favors glucagon. Hepatic glucose production supports circulating glucose during fasting.

quizzes.question: Which organ is a major direct target for glucagon’s glucose-raising effect?
options: The mature red blood cell exports glycogen as glucose.
The thyroid converts glucagon into T4.
The kidney is the only glucagon target.
The liver responds by increasing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
quizzes.rationale: Falling glucose favors glucagon. Hepatic glucose production supports circulating glucose during fasting.

studyNotes.title: Hormone Signaling and Feedback
studyNotes.summary: Endocrine systems coordinate distant targets through hormone release, receptor binding, and feedback regulation.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Hormone classes
Peptide hormones generally bind cell-surface receptors. Steroid and thyroid hormones can act through intracellular receptors. Receptor distribution determines target responsiveness.

### Feedback and timing
Negative feedback limits upstream drive. Pulsatile and circadian secretion patterns add information, so timing matters when interpreting levels.

### Axis organization
Hypothalamic and pituitary signals regulate peripheral glands. Stress, sleep, nutrition, and life stage modify endocrine axes.
keyPoints: Hormone effect depends on receptors and target context.
Negative feedback limits excess axis activity.
Secretion can be pulsatile or circadian.
Hormone class influences receptor location.
mnemonics: Hypothalamus → pituitary → gland, with feedback upward.

studyNotes.title: Metabolic and Stress Hormones
studyNotes.summary: Hormones coordinate fuel availability, metabolic rate, and responses to stress.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Glucose regulation
Insulin supports nutrient uptake and storage in responsive tissues; glucagon promotes hepatic glucose output during fasting.

### Thyroid hormones
T3 and T4 influence metabolic activity, growth, and development. TSH responds to hypothalamic signals and circulating thyroid hormone feedback.

### Adrenal hormones
Cortisol supports longer-term stress adaptation and substrate availability. Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium handling; catecholamines act rapidly.
keyPoints: Insulin generally favors nutrient storage and use.
Glucagon supports hepatic fuel mobilization during fasting.
Thyroid hormones influence metabolism and development.
Cortisol and aldosterone have distinct adrenal roles.
mnemonics: Insulin stores; glucagon mobilizes hepatic fuel.

studyNotes.title: Reproductive Physiology
studyNotes.summary: Reproductive function relies on coordinated gonadotropin signaling, gonadal hormones, and feedback across life stages.
studyNotes.contentMarkdown:
### Gonadal axis
GnRH stimulates pituitary LH and FSH. These signals regulate steroid production and gamete development.

### Ovarian cycle
Follicular estradiol patterns influence feedback. Sustained high estradiol can produce positive feedback and an LH surge; luteal progesterone supports the endometrium.

### Testicular function
LH supports Leydig-cell testosterone production. FSH acts on Sertoli-cell functions that support spermatogenesis. Timing and life stage influence hormone measurements.
keyPoints: GnRH regulates LH and FSH.
LH and FSH act on different gonadal cell functions.
Estradiol feedback varies with cycle phase and pattern.
Hormone interpretation depends on timing and life stage.
mnemonics: LH: Leydig; FSH: Sertoli in testes.
